Meanwhile, somewhere in rural northern Malawi...

By: Johann Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
About 30% of Malawi's population are living in South Africa - but what effect is this having on the villages where they came from?

Summary:
For more than a century migrant workers from Malawi have been streaming to South Africa, with devastating effects on the villages where they came from. Typically the men come to look for work. Those who go home over holiday periods take some money back, but they've also taken HIV/Aids to these vulnerable communities, where health care is virtually non-existent. Even worse -most of the men lose contact with their families back home, prompting the women to also come to SA, to try and find their husbands.But, because these women don't have official papers or money for the bus fare, many of them unknowingly fall prey to ruthless human traffickers. If they survive the journey, with illegal border crossings (walking through Kruger etc) they end up in Diepsloot as illegal immigrants, and the people who brought them claim ownership of these women, as they can't pay the money for the bus trip. These women are then forced into prostitution, or simply sold off to willing men for a few hundred rand.

Press Release:


Malawi Migration
Almost one third of Malawi’s population lives and works in South Africa. But for migrants, the week-long bus trip from remote Malawian villages to South African cities is treacherous and fraught with danger. Often at the mercy of ruthless human traffickers, travellers face illegal border crossings, robberies and sexual abuse. While some make it to the bright lights of Johannesburg, others are never heard from again. Carte Blanche documents the long journey to a new life.


Script:


Johannesburg, city of gold. For millions of people in the deep rural areas of South Africa and the neighbouring countries, it is the city of dreams – a place to find work and escape from the poverty they were born into. But although shiny from a distance, another reality waits inside this beast
V/O It is called Human Trafficking. This disturbing mob murder happend at the end of 2015 and the victim was from Malawi.
Bongani The attack happened here at Diepsloot, and the obvious assumption is to think that this was just another xenophobic attack. But not according to witnesses who say it was a jealous malawian husband who set the mob onto the victim who's a transporter, and they are the people who bring folks from Malawi to Johni as they call Gauteng.
Bongani link outside consulate For the Malawian Government this situation couldn't be more serious and they have done everything in their power to help us pursue this investigation, especially on the Malawian side.
Bongani inside the High Commission How many Malawians are in South Africa today?
Professor I don’t have a real figure yet, I’ve heard of projections of 6 million or 5 million but actually we don't have, we don't have any records of how many Malawians are here
V/O That is, almost a third of the country’s entire 18 million population. The reason they don't have exact figures is because the majority of Malawians here are not on the system as they entered the country illegaly
Professor I am sure that most of the Malawians that are here has come here as a result of human trafficking
V/O Charles Luhanga did not. He came to South Africa 20 years ago and today he is textile manager at a large retail shop in Pretoria. Most of his salary is sent to Malawi every month
Charles I come from Mzimba, thats the boma. But Im coming from Chief Chindi.
V/O "Charles invited us to come with him to Mzimba, to investigate the human trafficking of especially Malawian women to South Africa. The majority of people living in the Mzimba district are hovering on the brink of famine, with unemployment almost 100%. In the town of Mzimba we see people crowding, even sleeping on the pavement, waiting for the maize imported from Zambia. A 20kg bag of maize will have to last a family of 10 up to a month, often as their only food.

On the way to Charles’ village we stop at the local clinic serving his area. His mother-in-law was brought 50km to here with an ox-cart as she is suffering from Malaria. Her own family came with to assist her, which is just as well as they’ve now been waiting 3 days with no doctor or even a nurse in sight.

Most of the houses we see were built with money sent from South Africa, but it comes at a price, as there are very few working aged men left to do the things men are needed for.

Charles’ family was not expecting him because communication from South Africa is difficult. Like most men, he can only come here once a year, at best. They offered to slaughter a chicken for us but we have to move on, and only stay an hour. His whole extended family of around 30 people are totally dependant on Charles’ money which he sends every month from his salary.

In this village on the way back to Mzimba, we again find only women and old men, all of the women in this village are now divorced because as the years went on, their husbands simply disappeared into South Africa.

And this is when many women out of sheer desperation then decide to also go to Johni. To look for their husbands or earn some money themselves. Leaving their children and their elders behind.

If you only speak ChiTimbuka and have never been out of your deep rural village, going to Johannesburg is a leap into another dimension. Made worse if you don't have any legal papers or any money. This has led to a whole industry of transporters, specialising in getting them there. Unfortunately these are often the traffickers


"
whos only aim is to deceive, lure and exploit these vulnerable people.

Link Bongani So this is the deal: The transporter offers to take the woman to South Africa to find her husband or to get her a job. As payment he takes whatever money she may have, with the difference to be sorted out later. Once on the journey she is completely in his control, indebted and in trouble, she may even be forced to have sex with him or the driver on the way to prevent her from being offloaded in a strange country and to ensure protection when they cross the border.
V/O Febi was one of a number of women who told us about forced sex on the journey
Febi, speaks in ChiTimbuka, with english subtitels I refused because my body was not even accepting to be touced, but I had no choice, as I’m a woman. I failed to fight back. Then we slept together.
V/O Another danger waits around the Beit Bridge border. Groups of thugs called the amagumaguma. Marcel van der Watt has been investigating trafficking for years.
Marcel Basically what these guys are, is just bandits, criminals, often implicated in rape, robbery, there’s been accounts of murder
V/O They target people jumping the border. When Febi arrived at the Beit Bridge border she and a friend was given money to bribe their way through because they had slept with the driver
Febi, speaks in ChiTimbuka, with english subtitels The transporter gave it to me to show inside the migration office. Of all my friends he only gave two of us R2000 to show. But all my friends without passports he told them to jump.
V/O "The rest of the group who had to jump, ran into the amagumaguma. Everyone ran for their lives. This man and woman were caught, told to undress, sjamboked, and forced to have sex. Neither of them were ever seen again.

Febi found only later that she was pregnant and had contracted HIV/Aids, a tragedy echoed by many of the women we interviewed.

Nelson Ndlovo was working in South Africa and when he started missing his wife and 1-yr old son too much he asked them to come with a transporter and join him. Days after their departure, he received a phone call saying that the bodies of his wife and baby son were found in the bush on the Zim side of the Beit Bridge border. He had to pay for the bodies to be sent back to Malawi for the burial and he left South Africa in such a rush that he didn’t even pack for the journey . When he arrived, his uncle would not allow him to view the bodies. Both his wife and son’s private parts were missing, presumably cut off by the amagumaguma for the muti market."
Nelson Ndlovu The body was not looking nice.The child was cut here.
V/O We walked to their graves, deep in the bush, they could not separate the mutilated bodies and had to bury them in the same grave, leaving the other one empty. This added to the trauma of the whole family.
Brother in law Our culture does not allow two bodies in one grave and a body must have all its parts or culture proposes
V/O Nelson is so disturbed that he has not been able to return to South Africa to work and spends his days wondering the hills around the village. His whole family now lost their only source of income.
Link Bongani Even if you survive the perilous journey, your troubles may just be starting. This is Beyers Naude drive in Honeydew. Now, to the untrained eye, on the other side of the road are ladies selling blankets, clothes and other household items but the initiated ones will tell you many of the women are themselves for sale, for an hour, a night, as prostitutes, or even permanently as wife or slaves. You just have to negotiate a price with the transporter.


V/O To prove the point, Charles went in enquiring about buying a wife. The transporters offered to rather bring him “a clean or fresh one” from malawi
Charles Then they told me that you need to give us R3500 which is without passport then they will arrange within 3 days. I said, ok, if its 3 days then how do I get her? Because there are some problems on the way in terms of Police not finding us? They said don't worry about that, we will arrange that.
V/O But in the mean time for R50, he could take one for the night. We took her to a safe house, told her who we were and she told us her story.
Ellen I came here in 2013. I came with a transporter. She charged me 50,000. With this Ill take you to Jonhi. The transporter promised her a job in South Africa. Once in Mozambique she ordered Ellen to go and sleep with the driver in exchange for food for the trip.
Ellen I asked the question: on the way are you going to buy me food? he said: no problem the food we will buy for you. These people they just bought me once the food eto eat, once!
V/O When she reached Johannesburg, she realised that her destiny was not what she expected.
Ellen When we reached Honeydew there are so many men waiting there as if there is a gathering. You hear me? Then those men they talk to the transporter. This one, I like her. This one I like her. This one I like her. The the transporter calls you. They say: This one knows you.
V/O There was no sign of the house job she was promised. She was expected to earn her keep by sleeping with the men who came into the local tavern. The transporter would negotiate the price and she would have no say in whether she wants to do this or not. Now its 2.5 years later and nothing has changed.
Ellen I cant remember how many men I have slept with.
V/O Ellen misses her two little children back home, not knowing if they even have food and she hasn't earned any money to send home.
Ellen The whole family depends on me. I came here to look for a job so that I can help my people at home. If I can find R1000 and send that money home so that the can buy a tin of maize and vegetables and buy fish. But if me, I am struggling this side, how can that family be helped. There is no help.
V/O What we found here, not only goes for Malawians. Mozambicans, Zimbabweans and many other Africans are being trafficked to South Africa. The problem has become so serious that our first Act to combat Human Trafficking was introduced 8 months ago. But its implementation faces many challenges, and it is still too early to tell if it will make a difference.

The transporters offered to rather bring him “a clean or fresh one” from malawi Charles Then they told me that you need to give us R3500 which is without passport then they will arrange within 3 days. I said, ok, if its 3 days then how do I get her? Because there are some problems on the way in terms of Police not finding us? They said don't worry about that, we will arrange that. V/O But in the mean time for R50, he could take one for the night. We took her to a safe house, told her who we were and she told us her story. Ellen I came here in 2013. I came with a transporter. She charged me 50,000. With this Ill take you to Jonhi. The transporter promised her a job in South Africa. Once in Mozambique she ordered Ellen to go and sleep with the driver in exchange for food for the trip. Ellen I asked the question: on the way are you going to buy me food? he said: no problem the food we will buy for you. These people they just bought me once the food eto eat, once! V/O When she reached Johannesburg, she realised that her destiny was not what she expected. Ellen When we reached Honeydew there are so many men waiting there as if there is a gathering. You hear me? Then those men they talk to the transporter. This one, I like her. This one I like her. This one I like her. The the transporter calls you. They say: This one knows you. V/O There was no sign of the house job she was promised. She was expected to earn her keep by sleeping with the men who came into the local tavern. The transporter would negotiate the price and she would have no say in whether she wants to do this or not. Now its 2.5 years later and nothing has changed. Ellen I cant remember how many men I have slept with. V/O Ellen misses her two little children back home, not knowing if they even have food and she hasn't earned any money to send home. Ellen The whole family depends on me. I came here to look for a job so that I can help my people at home. If I can find R1000 and send that money home so that the can buy a tin of maize and vegetables and buy fish. But if me, I am struggling this side, how can that family be helped. There is no help. V/O What we found here, not only goes for Malawians. Mozambicans, Zimbabweans and many other Africans are being trafficked to South Africa. The problem has become so serious that our first Act to combat Human Trafficking was introduced 8 months ago. But its implementation faces many challenges, and it is still too early to tell if it will make a difference.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): About 30% of Malawi's population are living in South Africa - but what effect is this having on the villages where they came from?
metadata.Summary: For more than a century migrant workers from Malawi have been streaming to South Africa, with devastating effects on the villages where they came from. Typically the men come to look for work. Those who go home over holiday periods take some money back, but they've also taken HIV/Aids to these vulnerable communities, where health care is virtually non-existent. Even worse -most of the men lose contact with their families back home, prompting the women to also come to SA, to try and find their husbands.But, because these women don't have official papers or money for the bus fare, many of them unknowingly fall prey to ruthless human traffickers. If they survive the journey, with illegal border crossings (walking through Kruger etc) they end up in Diepsloot as illegal immigrants, and the people who brought them claim ownership of these women, as they can't pay the money for the bus trip. These women are then forced into prostitution, or simply sold off to willing men for a few hundred rand.
